claim: Mutations in the adult β-globin gene can lead to a variety of hemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia.
source: Mutations in the adult β-globin gene can lead to a variety of hemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about hemoglobinopathies.

claim: An increase in fetal hemoglobin expression throughout adulthood (hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, HPFH) has been found to ameliorate hemoglobinopathies.
source: An increase in fetal hemoglobin expression throughout adulthood, a condition named hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH), has been found to ameliorate hemoglobinopathies.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Deletional HPFH occurs through the excision of a significant portion of the 3′ end of the β-globin locus, including a CTCF binding site termed 3′HS1.
source: Deletional HPFH occurs through the excision of a significant portion of the 3′ end of the β-globin locus, including a CTCF binding site termed 3′HS1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about deletional HPFH.

claim: Deletion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site alone induces fetal hemoglobin expression in both adult CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and HUDEP-2 erythroid progenitor cells.
source: Here, we show that the deletion of this CTCF site alone induces fetal hemoglobin expression in both adult CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and HUDEP-2 erythroid progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The induction of fetal hemoglobin by 3′HS1 deletion is driven by the ectopic access of a distal enhancer located in the OR52A1 gene downstream of the locus.
source: This induction is driven by the ectopic access of a previously postulated distal enhancer located in the OR52A1 gene downstream of the locus, which can also be insulated by the inversion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing deletion of the HPFH enhancer in OR52A1 reduces HBG expression in Figure 3.

claim: The distal enhancer in OR52A1 can be insulated by the inversion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site.
source: This induction is driven by the ectopic access of a previously postulated distal enhancer located in the OR52A1 gene downstream of the locus, which can also be insulated by the inversion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing 3′HS1 inversion reduces HBG expression in Figure 1.

claim: Genetic editing of the 3′HS1 binding site can have therapeutic implications to treat hemoglobinopathies.
source: This suggests that genetic editing of this binding site can have therapeutic implications to treat hemoglobinopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The human β-globin locus consists of five globin genes embedded in the olfactory receptor cluster.
source: The human β-globin locus consists of five globin genes embedded in the olfactory receptor cluster.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the β-globin locus structure.

claim: During early development, globin genes undergo gene switching from embryonic ε-globin (HBE) to fetal γ-globin (HBG1/2) and finally to adult β-globin (HBB).
source: During early development, these globin genes undergo gene switching from embryonic ε-globin (HBE) to fetal γ-globin (HBG1/2) and finally to adult β-globin (HBB).
evidence: This is established knowledge about globin gene switching during development.

claim: Inherited mutations in the HBB gene lead to dysfunction of the adult β-globin protein, causing hemoglobinopathies.
source: Inherited mutations in the HBB gene lead to dysfunction of the adult β-globin protein, causing hemoglobinopathies (Bauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The symptoms of hemoglobinopathies can be alleviated by persistent expression of fetal hemoglobin throughout adulthood.
source: The symptoms of these disorders, including sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia, can be alleviated by persistent expression of fetal hemoglobin (hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin [HPFH]) throughout adulthood, which compensates for the mutant adult β-globin (Bank, 2006; Hassell, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Multiple genome-editing strategies have been proposed to mimic HPFH as a treatment for hemoglobinopathies.
source: As such, multiple genome-editing strategies have been proposed to mimic HPFH as a treatment for hemoglobinopathies (Bauer et al., 2012; Breda et al., 2016; Sankaran et al., 2008; Sankaran et al., 2011; Sankaran et al., 2009; Traxler et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2011; Ye et al., 2016; Zeng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Non-deletional HPFH is caused by point mutations in the BCL11A binding site at the HBG1/2 promoters.
source: First is the non-deletional HPFH caused by point mutations in the BCL11A binding site at the HBG1/2 promoters, and disruption of this transcriptional repressor binding leads to the activation of these genes (Forget, 1998; Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2018; Traxler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Deletional HPFH consists of the excision of a large genomic region within the β-globin locus, frequently including HBB and HBD.
source: Second is the deletional HPFH that consists of the excision of a large genomic region within the β-globin locus, frequently including HBB and HBD (Forget, 1998; Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It remains unclear how deletional HPFH deletions lead to the expression of fetal globin in adulthood.
source: These deletions can vary in length, and it remains unclear as to how they lead to the expression of fetal globin in adulthood (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The human β-globin gene locus is flanked by five CTCF binding sites (CBSs), which form the anchors for six chromosomal loops.
source: The human β-globin gene locus is flanked by five CTCF binding sites (CBSs), which form the anchors for six chromosomal loops (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Two convergent CBSs, designated as 3′HS1 and HS5, are located at the borders of the globin gene cluster.
source: Two convergent CBSs, designated as 3′HS1 and HS5, are located at the borders of the globin gene cluster.
evidence: This is a description of the genomic architecture shown in Figure 1.

claim: HPFH deletions frequently cover the 3′HS1 CBS.
source: The HPFH deletions frequently cover the 3′HS1 CBS (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the figure showing HPFH deletion regions.

claim: Deletion of the HS5 CTCF site in K562 cells resulted in the upregulation of the 3′ genes including HBB and HBG1/2.
source: We observed that deletion of the HS5 CTCF site resulted in the upregulation of the 3′ genes including HBB and HBG1/2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The disruption of 3′HS1 CBS in K562 cells led solely to the upregulation of HBG1/2.
source: Interestingly, the disruption of 3′HS1 CBS led solely to the upregulation of HBG1/2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Altering the CTCF binding profile across the β-globin locus can significantly change the expression of the β-globin genes.
source: These results show that altering the CTCF binding profile across the locus can significantly change the expression of the β-globin genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results in K562 cells.

claim: In situ Hi-C data was generated with high resolution at 5 kb.
source: In situ Hi-C data was generated with high resolution at 5 kb.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: A total of 15,207–16,529 loops could be detected in the HUDEP-2 clones used for in situ Hi-C using Mustache.
source: A total of 15,207–16,529 loops could be detected in the HUDEP-2 clones used for in situ Hi-C using Mustache (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Roayaei Ardakany et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from Hi-C analysis.

claim: The CTCF bound around the β-globin locus form four chromosomal loops and separate the cluster into three distinct domains.
source: The CTCF bound around the β-globin locus form four chromosomal loops and separate the cluster into three distinct domains (Figure 1A and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in the figures.

claim: Enhancer to target gene interaction between the LCR and the HBB gene could be detected.
source: Of notice, we could detect the enhancer to target gene interaction between the LCR and the HBB gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in the figure.

claim: All HUDEP-2 clones have chromosome number 49–50,XY, which is of normal range in unmodified HUDEP-2 cells.
source: We also tested the copy number variance (CNV) in the three particular HUDEP-2 clones, we could verify all clones have chromosome number 49–50,XY, which is of normal range in unmodified HUDEP-2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Moir-Meyer et al., 2018; Vinjamur and Bauer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by CNV analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: In the 3′HS1 deletion clone, the loss of CTCF at 3′HS1 resulted in the total loss of loops between 3′HS1 and HS5.
source: In the 3′HS1 deletion clone, the loss of CTCF at 3′HS1 resulted in the total loss of loops between 3′HS1 and HS5 as well as loops between 3′HS1 and 5′-OR51B5-CBSs (not called as loop).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: In the 3′HS1 deletion clone, a strong increase in the interaction between HS5 and 3′-OR51A5-CBS was observed.
source: Concomitantly, a strong increase in the interaction between HS5 and 3′-OR51A5-CBS was observed (Figure 1D and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in the figures.

claim: The loss of a CTCF anchor drastically alters the 3D chromatin organization in the β-globin locus.
source: This reveals how the loss of a CTCF anchor drastically alters the 3D chromatin organization in the β-globin locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hi-C data showing changes in chromatin loops.

claim: The inversion of the 3′HS1 CTCF caused a significant increase in the interaction between 3′HS1 and 3′-OR52A5 CBS.
source: The inversion of the 3′HS1 CTCF caused a significant increase in the interaction between 3′HS1 and 3′-OR52A5 CBS.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: In 3′HS1 inversion clones, 3′HS1 upstream interactions with HS5 and 5′-OR51B5-CBSs were decreased.
source: Meanwhile, 3′HS1 upstream interactions with HS5 and 5′-OR51B5-CBSs were decreased (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in the figures.

claim: The inversion of 3′HS1 CTCF drives the formation of chromosomal loops between the convergent CBSs, which may lead to stronger insulation of regulatory elements.
source: This revealed that the inversion of 3′HS1 CTCF drove the formation of chromosomal loops between the convergent CBSs, which may lead to stronger insulation of regulatory elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hi-C data and understanding of CTCF function.

claim: The HBG1/2 and HBE genes upregulated 2.5- to 8-fold in the Δ3′HS1 clones.
source: Next, we evaluated the expression of the β-globin genes and found that the HBG1/2 and HBE genes upregulated 2.5- to 8-fold in the Δ3′HS1 clones (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figures.

claim: The inversion of 3′HS1 resulted in a >50% reduction of HBE and near-complete depletion of HBG1/2.
source: In contrast, the inversion of 3′HS1 resulted in a >50% reduction of HBE and near-complete depletion of HBG1/2 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure.

claim: The increase in HBG1/2 upon deletion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site leads to a significant increase in fetal hemoglobin HbF.
source: Most notably, the increase in HBG1/2 upon deletion of the 3′HS1 CTCF site leads to a significant increase in fetal hemoglobin HbF (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in the figure.

claim: An increase in HbF+ cells from 4.3% in the Cas9 control clone to 37.8% and 53.1% in Δ3′HS1 B6 and D3 clones, respectively, was observed.
source: Consequently, we evaluated the clones for HbF+ cells by flow cytometry. Consistent with transcription level, we observed an increase in HbF+ cells from 4.3% in the Cas9 control clone to 37.8% and 53.1% in Δ3′HS1 B6 and D3 clones, respectively (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the figure.

claim: Inversion of 3′HS1 resulted in a decrease of HbF+ cells to below 1%.
source: Meanwhile, inversion of 3′HS1 resulted in a decrease of HbF+ cells to below 1%.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Deletion of the upstream HS5 CBS did not induce nor abrogate the quantity of HbF+ cells.
source: In contrast, deletion of the upstream HS5 CBS did not induce nor abrogate the quantity of HbF+ cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the figure.

claim: Following 3′HS1 CBS deletion, significant open chromatin was observed at the HBG1/2, BGLT3, and HBBP1 genes.
source: Following 3′HS1 CBS deletion, we observed significant open chromatin at the HBG1/2, BGLT3, and HBBP1 genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: There was a significant increase in activating H3K27ac in the HBG2 gene body following 3′HS1 CBS deletion.
source: There was also a significant increase in activating H3K27ac in the HBG2 gene body.
evidence: This is supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Epigenetic changes upon deletion of 3′HS1 CBS do not occur at the promoter of HBG2.
source: Interestingly, these epigenetic changes upon deletion of 3′HS1 CBS do not occur at the promoter of HBG2, which suggests that this 3′HS1-dependent regulation is independent from BCL11A transcriptional regulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data and is an inference about the mechanism.

claim: 161 upregulated and 153 downregulated genes were found in the Δ3′HS1 clones.
source: We found 161 upregulated and 153 downregulated genes in the Δ3′HS1 clones with HBG1/2 genes being the most significantly upregulated as well as β-globin cluster genes HBE1, HBBP, and BGLT3 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: HBG1/2 genes were the most significantly upregulated in the Δ3′HS1 clones.
source: We found 161 upregulated and 153 downregulated genes in the Δ3′HS1 clones with HBG1/2 genes being the most significantly upregulated as well as β-globin cluster genes HBE1, HBBP, and BGLT3 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: In the 3′HS1 inversion clones, only 3 upregulated genes and 51 downregulated genes were identified.
source: In the 3′HS1 inversion clones, we identified only 3 upregulated genes and 51 downregulated genes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claim: In 3′HS1 inversion clones, downregulation of HBG2 and upregulation of the nearby OR52A5 gene was observed.
source: In these clones, we observed downregulation of HBG2 and upregulation of the nearby OR52A5 gene; however, we did not observe any change in the expression of known γ-globin regulators (BCL11A, ZBTB7A (LRF), ELF2AK1 (HRI), ATF4, ZNF410, and NFIX) (Figure 2B and D, Supplementary file 1; Grevet et al., 2018; Masuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: No change in the expression of known γ-globin regulators (BCL11A, ZBTB7A (LRF), ELF2AK1 (HRI), ATF4, ZNF410, and NFIX) was observed in 3′HS1 inversion clones.
source: In these clones, we observed downregulation of HBG2 and upregulation of the nearby OR52A5 gene; however, we did not observe any change in the expression of known γ-globin regulators (BCL11A, ZBTB7A (LRF), ELF2AK1 (HRI), ATF4, ZNF410, and NFIX) (Figure 2B and D, Supplementary file 1; Grevet et al., 2018; Masuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: No significant reduction in BCL11A protein level was observed in Δ3′HS1 clones by immunoblotting.
source: We further verified BCL11A protein level by immunoblotting and observed no significant reduction in Δ3′HS1 clones (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in the figure.

claim: BCL11A does not contribute to the induction of HbF in the edited HUDEP-2 cells.
source: Taken together, we concluded that BCL11A does not contribute to the induction of HbF in the edited HUDEP-2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq and Western blot data showing no change in BCL11A.

claim: Targeted disruption of a BCL11A gene enhancer in both WT and Δ3′HS1 HUDEP-2 clones resulted in significantly lower BCL11A expression.
source: To further elucidate the role of BCL11A in the regulation of HBG1/2, we performed targeted disruption of a known BCL11A gene enhancer in both WT and Δ3′HS1 HUDEP-2 clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Bauer et al., 2013). This mutation resulted in a significantly lower BCL11A expression, and we observed further increase of HBG1/2 expression level and HbF+ cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: BCL11A enhancer disruption resulted in further increase of HBG1/2 expression level and HbF+ cells in Δ3′HS1 clones.
source: This mutation resulted in a significantly lower BCL11A expression, and we observed further increase of HBG1/2 expression level and HbF+ cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: Pomalidomide treatment of HUDEP-2 3′HS1 deletion clones resulted in a significant reduction in BCL11A protein.
source: Pomalidomide was found to boost the level of HbF in adult erythroblasts by destabilizing the BCL11A protein in cells (Grevet et al., 2018). Therefore, we treated HUDEP-2 3′HS1 deletion clones with pomalidomide and observed a significant reduction in BCL11A protein.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pomalidomide treatment led to further increase in expression of fetal globin in 3′HS1 deletion clones.
source: Therefore, we treated HUDEP-2 3′HS1 deletion clones with pomalidomide and observed a significant reduction in BCL11A protein. This led to further increase in expression of fetal globin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Genetic editing of the regulatory cis-element (3′HS1 CBS) accentuates with depletion of the transcriptional repressor BCL11A.
source: These results show that genetic editing of the regulatory cis-element (3′HS1 CBS) accentuates with depletion of the transcriptional repressor BCL11A.
evidence: This is an inference based on the additive effects of 3′HS1 deletion and BCL11A depletion.

claim: The γ-globin activation in 3′HS1 deletion HUDEP-2 cells was not driven by the BCL11A-associated pathways.
source: This further indicates that the γ-globin activation in 3′HS1 deletion HUDEP-2 cells was not driven by the BCL11A-associated pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that BCL11A levels do not change with 3′HS1 deletion.

claim: The double disruption of BCL11A and 3′HS1 led to similar level of γ-globin activation as the disruption of BCL11A alone.
source: The double disruption of BCL11A and 3′HS1 also led to similar level of γ-globin activation as the disruption of BCL11A alone (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: 3′HS1-regulated γ-globin repression might be hypostatic to the BCL11A-mediated γ-globin repression.
source: This data suggests that 3′HS1-regulated γ-globin repression might be hypostatic to the BCL11A-mediated γ-globin repression.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the epistasis experiment results.

claim: The OR52A1 region is bound by the GATA1 transcriptional activator in the erythroid lineages.
source: We then analyzed the ATAC-seq, GATA1 ChIP-seq data together to search for potential cis-regulatory elements. We found the OR52A1 region bound by the GATA1 transcriptional activator in the erythroid lineages (Corces et al., 2016; Feingold and Forget; Liu et al., 2018; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by GATA1 ChIP-seq data shown in the figure and citations.

claim: A previously described HPFH enhancer encompasses both OR52A1 gene and GATA1 binding site.
source: Importantly, the mapping of a previously described HPFH enhancer encompassed both OR52A1 gene and GATA1 binding site (Elder et al., 1990; Feingold and Forget, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of the GATA1 binding site within the HPFH enhancer in Δ3′HS1 clones reduced the HBG1/2 expression and HbF+ cell percentage.
source: We proceeded to delete the GATA1 binding site within the HPFH enhancer site and the entire HPFH enhancer marked by ATAC-seq in Δ3′HS1 clones (Figure 3B). We found that both deletions reduced the HBG1/2 expression and HbF+ cell percentage in these cells, suggesting that the HPFH enhancer contributes to the activation of HBG1/2 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Deletion of the entire HPFH enhancer in Δ3′HS1 clones reduced the HBG1/2 expression and HbF+ cell percentage.
source: We proceeded to delete the GATA1 binding site within the HPFH enhancer site and the entire HPFH enhancer marked by ATAC-seq in Δ3′HS1 clones (Figure 3B). We found that both deletions reduced the HBG1/2 expression and HbF+ cell percentage in these cells, suggesting that the HPFH enhancer contributes to the activation of HBG1/2 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The HPFH enhancer contributes to the activation of HBG1/2.
source: We found that both deletions reduced the HBG1/2 expression and HbF+ cell percentage in these cells, suggesting that the HPFH enhancer contributes to the activation of HBG1/2 (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing reduced HBG expression upon HPFH enhancer deletion.

claim: Mildly increased v4C signal in HBG2 promoter region of Δ3′HS1 cells compared with WT and 3′HS1 inversion clones was observed when HPFH enhancer region acts as viewpoint.
source: We further evaluated whether there were direct interactions between HBG1/2 and HPFH enhancer after the deletion of 3′HS1 by virtual 4C (v4C) in our Hi-C dataset. We observed mildly increased v4C signal in HBG2 promoter region of Δ3′HS1 cells compared with WT and 3′HS1 inversion clones when HPFH enhancer region acts as viewpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by virtual 4C analysis of Hi-C data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Mildly increased v4C signal in HPFH enhancer region of Δ3′HS1 cells compared with WT and 3′HS1 inversion clones was observed when HBG2 promoter region acts as viewpoint.
source: Vice versa, we also observed mildly increased v4C signal in HPFH enhancer region of Δ3′HS1 cells compared with WT and 3′HS1 inversion clones when HBG2 promoter region acts as viewpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by virtual 4C analysis of Hi-C data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The deletion of 3′HS1 might have induced more frequent interaction between HPFH enhancer and HBG2 promoter regions.
source: These data suggest that the deletion of 3′HS1 might have induced more frequent interaction between HPFH enhancer and HBG2 promoter regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the virtual 4C data.

claim: Mouse and human β-globin locus and its surrounding regions have been shown to be evolutionally conserved.
source: Previously, mouse and human β-globin locus and its surrounding regions have been shown to be evolutionally conserved (Bulger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Disruption of 3′HS1 site in mouse did not result in any change in the β-like globin gene expression.
source: More interestingly, previous report showed that the disruption of 3′HS1 site in mouse did not result in any change in the β-like globin gene expression (Bender et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mouse and rat homolog of human OR52A1–Olfr68 bears two single-nucleotide substitutions right at the core binding site of GATA1.
source: Therefore, we evaluated the evolutionary conservation of OR52A1 in mammals and found mouse and rat homolog of human OR52A1–Olfr68 bears two single-nucleotide substitutions right at the core binding site of GATA1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figure.

claim: GATA1 binding is absent in the OR52A1's homolog Olfr68 and its surrounding region in mouse erythroid cells.
source: When we further checked the GATA1 ChIP-seq in mouse erythroid cells, we also found the absence of binding in the OR52A1's homolog Olfr68 and its surrounding region (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by GATA1 ChIP-seq data in mouse cells shown in the figure.

claim: The loss of GATA1 binding in mouse explains the difference between mouse and human on the effect of 3′HS1 deletion on globin gene expression.
source: This data suggests that the mouse olfactory receptor region 3′ to β-globin genes no longer bears GATA1 binding sites and enhancer activity. Overall, the loss of GATA1 binding in mouse clearly explains the difference between mouse and human on the effect of 3′HS1 deletion on globin gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative genomics and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Moving the HPFH enhancer to the proximity of globin locus mildly increases the HBG1/2 gene expression by threefold with increase of HBE1 gene and reduction of HBB gene.
source: We used paired guide RNA to delete a 48 kb region between HPFH enhancer and 3′HS1, to access the effect of distance between enhancer and target genes in the presence of chromosomal insulators (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). We obtained a heterozygous clone bearing this 48 kb deletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). We found that moving the HPFH enhancer to the proximity of globin locus mildly increases the HBG1/2 gene expression by threefold with increase of HBE1 gene and reduction of HBB gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Both chromosomal distance and insulator contribute to the low expression of HBG1/2, but chromosomal insulators are dominant to insulate HPFH enhancer to access the globin genes.
source: Overall, the data suggests that both chromosomal distance and insulator contribute to the low expression of HBG1/2, but chromosomal insulators are dominant to insulate HPFH enhancer to access the globin genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results of the 48 kb deletion.

claim: High deletion percentage of both 3′HS1 and HS5 CBSs was achieved in primary CD34+ HSPC cells from three different donors.
source: To assess the therapeutic potential of 3′HS1 deletion in primary HSPCs, we performed the 3′HS1 and HS5 CBS deletions in adult mobilized peripheral blood CD34+ HSPC from three different donors (Figure 4A). We achieved high deletion percentage of both CBSs in these primary cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A robust increase in HbF+ cells across all three donors with 3′HS1 deletion but not with HS5 deletion was observed upon differentiation of primary CD34+ HSPCs.
source: Upon differentiation, we observed a robust increase in HbF+ cells across all three donors with 3′HS1 deletion but not with HS5 deletion (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the figures.

claim: Normal erythroid differentiation was not affected by either CBS deletion in primary CD34+ HSPCs.
source: The normal erythroid differentiation was not affected by either CBS deletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by differentiation analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The disruption of the 3'HS1 CBS in primary patient cells supports the involvement of a downstream cis-acting regulatory element on the HBG1/2 genes.
source: While the disruption of the 3'HS1 CBS in primary patient cells did not yield as great of an effect on HbF+ cells as in HUDEP-2 cells, the results do support the involvement of a downstream cis-acting regulatory element on the HBG1/2 genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the primary cell data.

claim: The 3′HS1 CBS modulates the HPFH enhancer's access to the HBG1/2 genes.
source: Finally, based on our data, we propose a model where the 3′HS1 CBS modulates the HPFH enhancer's access to the HBG1/2 genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on all the experimental data.

claim: The deletion of a CBS – 3′HS1– in the human β-globin locus can phenocopy HPFH.
source: Here, we show that the deletion of a CBS – 3′HS1– in the human β-globin locus can phenocopy HPFH.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: HPFH phenocopy by 3′HS1 deletion is driven by alteration of the 3D genomic organization around the β-globin locus, which allows the long-range interaction of a distal enhancer in the OR52A1 gene to drive the expression of HBG1/2.
source: This condition is driven by alteration of the 3D genomic organization around the β-globin locus, which allows the long-range interaction of a distal enhancer in the OR52A1 gene to drive the expression of HBG1/2.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on Hi-C and enhancer deletion experiments.

claim: Inversion of 3′HS1 insulates the enhancer element and further suppresses HBG1/2.
source: We further show that inversion of 3′HS1 insulates the enhancer element and further suppresses HBG1/2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced HBG expression in inversion clones.

claim: CTCF binding at the β-globin locus modulates the accessibility of the fetal HBG1/2 genes to a downstream enhancer.
source: Our study reveals how CTCF binding at this locus modulates the accessibility of the fetal HBG1/2 genes to a downstream enhancer.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: In the HPFH enhancer scenario, 3′HS1 limits the HPFH enhancer access to HBG1/2 by forming the sub-TAD with 5′HS.
source: In the HPFH enhancer scenario, 3′HS1 limits the HPFH enhancer access to HBG1/2 by forming the sub-TAD with 5′HS (Figure 4E; Oudelaar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on Hi-C data and supported by citation.

claim: When the 3′HS1 CBS is deleted, the HPFH enhancer gains access to HBG1/2 without the hinder of 3′HS1–HS5 loop.
source: When the 3′HS1 CBS is deleted, the HPFH enhancer gains access to HBG1/2 without the hinder of 3′HS1–HS5 loop.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on Hi-C and gene expression data.

claim: When the 3′HS1 CBS motif is inverted, the HPFH enhancer is further restricted by the pairing of 3′-OR52A5-CBS to the inverted 3′HS1 CBS, which results in strong chromosomal loop formation between the two CBSs.
source: When the 3′HS1 CBS motif is inverted, the HPFH enhancer is further restricted by the pairing of 3′-OR52A5-CBS to the inverted 3′HS1 CBS, which results in the strong chromosomal loop formation between the two CBSs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on Hi-C data showing increased loop formation.

claim: The insulation by 3′HS1 inversion leads to reduced HBG1/2 expression and upregulation of OR52A5.
source: This insulation leads to the reduced HBG1/2 expression and upregulation of OR52A5 (Figures 2B and 4E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: Other regulatory elements exist between 3′HS1 and 3′-OR52A5-CBS since only a partial decrease of HBG1/2 expression occurs with HPFH enhancer deletion in Δ3′HS1 cells.
source: Furthermore, we have elucidated the function of long speculated HPFH enhancer in the induction of HbF with our Δ3′HS1 cells. However, we suspect that other regulatory elements also exist between 3′HS1 and 3′-OR52A5-CBS since we only get a partial decrease of HBG1/2 expression with HPFH enhancer deletion in Δ3′HS1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete reduction of HBG expression upon HPFH enhancer deletion.

claim: Other previously identified HPFH enhancers may also contribute to HbF induction in the Δ3′HS1 cells.
source: This may suggest that other previously identified HPFH enhancers also contribute to HbF induction in the Δ3′HS1 cells (Feingold and Forget, 1989; Forget, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the incomplete effect of single enhancer deletion and supported by citations.

claim: Other GATA1 binding sites can be observed between OR52A1 and OR52A5 genes of erythroid progenitor cells.
source: Indeed, other GATA1 binding sites can be observed between OR52A1 and OR52A5 genes of erythroid progenitor cells.
evidence: This is an observation from ChIP-seq data.

claim: GATA1 binding across the locus works collectively to activate HBG1/2 expression with or without direct promoter-enhancer interactions.
source: Overall, these observations suggest that GATA1 binding across the locus works collectively to activate HBG1/2 expression with or without direct promoter-enhancer interactions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the presence of multiple GATA1 binding sites.

claim: TF binding disrupting nucleotide substitutions occur at the GATA1 binding site in HPFH enhancer in some mammal species that do not express distinct form of fetal hemoglobin (mouse and rat).
source: Interestingly, despite the evolution conservation of OR52A1 gene in mammals, TF binding disrupting nucleotide substitutions occur at the GATA1 binding site in HPFH enhancer in some mammal species that do not express distinct form of fetal hemoglobin (mouse and rat) (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and ChIP-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: HPFH enhancer may play a role in regulating globin expression in other developmental stages.
source: This evolutionary alteration in the TF binding site suggests that HPFH enhancer may also play a role in regulating globin expression in other developmental stages.
evidence: This is a speculation based on evolutionary conservation patterns.

claim: The potential function of HPFH enhancer may still need the modulation of 3D genomic reorganization.
source: The consistent binding of GATA1 in high HBE/HBG-expressing K562 cells and high HBB-expressing HUDEP-2 cells suggests that the potential function of HPFH enhancer may still need the modulation of 3D genomic reorganization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that GATA1 binding alone is not sufficient for activation.

claim: The deletion of 3′HS1 only induces a portion of cells to be F+ cells, with an interesting differentiation block phenotype in a large portion of clones.
source: Despite our data suggesting that deletion of 3′HS1 is sufficient to induce the γ-globin activation, yet, the upregulation does not completely phenocopy the HPFH condition, in which the HbF is expressed at pancellular level. The deletion of 3′HS1 only induces a portion of cells to be F+ cells, with an interesting differentiation block phenotype in a large portion of clones we have selected (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is an observation from flow cytometry data.

claim: The full HPFH phenotype may require the deletion of HBB and HBD genes to erase the strong enhancer-promoter interaction between LCR and HBB.
source: Although HUDEP-2 is known to be heterogenous in clonal level, the F+ cell phenotype of 3′HS1-deleted cells suggests that the full HPFH phenotype may require the deletion of HBB and HBD genes to erase the strong enhancer-promoter interaction between LCR and HBB.
evidence: This is a speculation about what is needed for full HPFH phenotype.

claim: The distance between HPFH enhancer and the globin locus could play a role in regulating γ-globin gene expression.
source: Furthermore, our results indicate that the distance between HPFH enhancer and the globin locus could also play a role in regulating γ-globin gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 48 kb deletion experiment.

claim: The deletion of both 3′HS1 and the flanking region between 3′HS1 and HPFH enhancer may activate the fetal hemoglobin to an even higher level.
source: This data hints that the deletion of both 3′HS1 and the flanking region between 3′HS1 and HPFH enhancer may activate the fetal hemoglobin to an even higher level.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the combined effects of insulator removal and distance reduction.

claim: Larger deletions will result in the reorganization of chromosomal loop interactions as well as the decrease of physical distance from HPFH enhancer to globin locus.
source: Larger deletions will result in the reorganization of chromosomal loop interactions as well as the decrease of physical distance from HPFH enhancer to globin locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of 3D genome organization.

claim: Enhancers have to locate at certain range of distance from the target gene promoters to exert the maximal activation effect.
source: The enhancers have to locate at certain range of distance from the target gene promoters to exert the maximal activation effect (Jessica Zuin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A method that can create large deletion that disrupts 3′HS1 and reduces enhancer-promoter distance simultaneously could be a potential gene therapy to effectively activate the γ-globin expression in hemoglobinopathies.
source: Therefore, a method that can create large deletion that disrupts 3′HS1 and reduces enhancer-promoter distance simultaneously could be a potential gene therapy to effectively activate the γ-globin expression in hemoglobinopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic proposal based on the experimental findings.
